descriptors.descriptor_basis: Interview transcript: G02 (Chief information officer, city council)

segments.title: Novel risks assimilated to standard IT governance
segments.quote: That's the same governance any major system gets and I'd resist the idea that it needs something special.
segments.full_text: Through the standard route. It's on the corporate risk register, it has a senior responsible owner, it reports into the digital board quarterly. That's the same governance any major system gets and I'd resist the idea that it needs something special. Once you start creating bespoke oversight for anything with a model in it, you end up with forty committees and no capacity.

codes.rationale: Governance is set by analogy to prior systems, without assessment of what is different about an adaptive model acting on the street.

segments.title: Concedes the oversight body cannot interrogate the model
segments.quote: Is that enough to interrogate a detection model in detail? No, probably not. What we do instead is rely on the vendor's assurance documentation and on the acceptance testing.
segments.full_text: It has me. And a non-executive with a technology background. Is that enough to interrogate a detection model in detail? No, probably not. What we do instead is rely on the vendor's assurance documentation and on the acceptance testing.

codes.rationale: Honest assessment of a capability gap in the respondent's own governance arrangement.
The mechanism for detecting problems is supplied by the party whose product would be found wanting.

segments.title: Algorithmic detail withheld as commercial confidence
segments.quote: Two asked for the algorithm and we refused those on commercial confidentiality grounds
segments.full_text: We've had — I want to say six or seven freedom of information requests. Most were about camera locations and we answered those. Two asked for the algorithm and we refused those on commercial confidentiality grounds, which is the vendor's position and legally sound.

codes.rationale: The information needed for public scrutiny is contractually unavailable, foreclosing informed engagement.

segments.title: Accepts the criticism as fair
segments.quote: That's a fair criticism and I'd expect it to be in the next one. The honest position is that in 2022 we weren't thinking about it, and by the time you're arguing about disclosure you've already signed
segments.full_text: I don't believe transparency terms were in the specification. That's a fair criticism and I'd expect it to be in the next one. The honest position is that in 2022 we weren't thinking about it, and by the time you're arguing about disclosure you've already signed.

codes.rationale: Acknowledgement without deflection, though it produces a commitment about future contracts rather than this one.
A foreseeable governance requirement was not built in at the only point where it was available.

segments.title: No identified route from complaint to parameter change
segments.quote: Whether transport can then change a parameter depends on the change-control terms, which — I'd have to look.
segments.full_text: There's the general complaints process. It routes to transport, not to us. Whether transport can then change a parameter depends on the change-control terms, which — I'd have to look. I don't know the answer to that off the top of my head, which I appreciate is not a great answer.

codes.rationale: The senior officer responsible cannot describe the path by which a resident's complaint could alter system behaviour.

summary: A governance account organised around treating the system as ordinary corporate IT. The respondent concedes that neither he nor the digital board can interrogate a detection model, and that assurance therefore rests on documentation supplied by the vendor. Algorithmic detail is withheld from freedom-of-information requests on commercial grounds — transparency terms were not in the specification, which he accepts as fair criticism. He cannot describe how a resident complaint could reach a system parameter.
transcript:
Interview transcript G02 — Chief information officer, city council
Case: Port Calder adaptive traffic signal and pedestrian detection system  |  SYNTHETIC DATA — not a real interview
[Interviewer] How does a system like this get governed once it's running?
[Respondent] Through the standard route. It's on the corporate risk register, it has a senior responsible owner, it reports into the digital board quarterly. That's the same governance any major system gets and I'd resist the idea that it needs something special. Once you start creating bespoke oversight for anything with a model in it, you end up with forty committees and no capacity.
[Interviewer] Does the digital board have the expertise to interrogate a model?
[Respondent] It has me. And a non-executive with a technology background. Is that enough to interrogate a detection model in detail? No, probably not. What we do instead is rely on the vendor's assurance documentation and on the acceptance testing.
[Interviewer] Has the public asked for information about the system?
[Respondent] We've had — I want to say six or seven freedom of information requests. Most were about camera locations and we answered those. Two asked for the algorithm and we refused those on commercial confidentiality grounds, which is the vendor's position and legally sound.
[Interviewer] Did the council consider negotiating that at procurement?
[Respondent] I don't believe transparency terms were in the specification. That's a fair criticism and I'd expect it to be in the next one. The honest position is that in 2022 we weren't thinking about it, and by the time you're arguing about disclosure you've already signed.
[Interviewer] Is there a route for a resident to challenge how a junction behaves?
[Respondent] There's the general complaints process. It routes to transport, not to us. Whether transport can then change a parameter depends on the change-control terms, which — I'd have to look. I don't know the answer to that off the top of my head, which I appreciate is not a great answer.
